title: Films portraying artists as normal people

commenti.body:
Reichardt and Hong Sang-soo are great examples. However all the biopics of famous XIX or XX century artists (all famous artists from the past) are inevitably tragic or extravagant... Except maybe Andrei Rublyev (Tarkovsky) or Poet (Omirbayev). 

According to your description, you should check out Contemplative Cinema, it's all about real people and real lives, within a real-life context and real occupations. Often played by non-actors...

 La vie de bohème (Kaurismaki); Nasumice (Burdeau)a photographer; Paterson (Jarmusch) a poet; Dong (Jia Zhangke) which is a documentary on a painter; Distant (Ceylan) a photographer; Le Filmeur (Cavalier) a filmmaker
I think you might really like As I Was Moving Ahead, Occasionally I Saw Brief Glimpses Of Beauty. You can find it online. It’s a time commitment, but it is also my personal favorite film.

I have an interesting addition to this setup for a film that portrays the artist in a normal way, albeit entrapped in extras or art circumstances beyond their control and ability to reason with—Barton Fink. If anything, I think it does an even better job of showing an artist as a normal person, as the titular character is talented, certainly, but it’s clear that half the film is about how strangely artists are treated in extremes of  being sycophantically worshipped for strange reasons alongside wide  albeit distanced  acclaimed, or straightforwardly exploited, devalued, and held in contract towards whatever’s chart. The whole early Hollywood phrasing certainly has plenty of its own flavor, and era-specific spin, but just about all of it holds true to the film industry and their greater precarious position of being an artist as a whole. 

More so, it answers a really important question in asking how to make a story about a writer and writing interesting, and it goes in a great direction of trying to chase down writers block, through seeing a number of truths about writing and whose stories get to be told and how the politics of voice align with writing, then ramping it up in a drastic turn to thriller-worthy genre fiction plots coming to life off the page.
[removed]

I think *American Splendor* (2003) qualifies. Harvey Pekar doesn't fit the mold of tortured artist. I mean, he is, in his way, but there is an overwhelming ordinariness to his life that serves as a counterpoint to his artistry. It's been a while since I've seen it, and it definitely merits a re-watch, but I remember it being a sensitive and nuanced portrayal of someone who didn't conform to the usual "creative-artist-as-mad-genius" stereotype. And it is a solid film, too.
[removed]

Reprise by Joachim trier. I'd say it's one of the best examples of how to do it when it comes to showing an artist's life. Without being too extravagant or over the top, it presents the story of two writer friends in a more humane way, I'd say.
Someone even called it Trainspotting but without the drugs. I can't agree more. Also it portrays male friendship in such a beautiful way 
Joachim has easily become one of my fav directors working today.

Jim Jarmusch’s Patterson is maybe a textbook example of this. A truck driver who writes poetry in his free time and is just a completely normal guy satisfied with his quiet humble life. Would highly recommend this movie btw. Underrated gem.

Have you seen The Banshees of Inisherin? It's not exactly what you're asking for but it's something I enjoyed as someone who agrees with what you're saying. One of the central themes/conflicts of the movie has to do with someone who believes artists need a special life and he rejects people for being too focused on daily living.
Bus driver*

Drive My Car follows a stage director as he struggles to make sense of his grief and shame. The movie integrates his artistic voice / expression with his personal drama but through a thoughtful roll up your sleeves and do the work perspective.

For instance, there are multiple scenes with him directing the actors at table reads and carefully breaking down and explaining his artistic goals.

Adam* Driver

To add something substantive to my lame joke: I agree with the parent above that Paterson is a great example of the OP’s request, but at the same time I experienced a conflicting observation while watching it. Specifically while the vehicle of the story was a very real working class life it played out like a fantasy — not in the sense that it was surreal but rather in that it depicted a life that I felt absolutely could not exist, at least not today. His life had so much dignity, his relationships with both his wife and coworkers were so authentic, and the life of the town surrounding him was so rich with life and humanity. Maybe it’s even my post-Covid jadedness but I couldn’t help thinking how impossible it was for his life to exist in our current reality.

Drive My Car (2022) is a beautiful story structured in a very realistic and process-driven way around the production of a play. Highly recommended. I don't think it overdramatizes anything, but some of its best moments come from its respect for the art and the artists.
I’ve seen Paterson and I absolutely love that movie. The scene where the little reads her poem to the character played by Adam Driver is so beautiful. :)

As an artist myself, I’ve a few favorites that captivate me and make me truly believe it.

Sudden Fear, Callas Forever, Something’s Gotta Give. And one that I kinda hate called The Divine Secrets of the Ya Ya Sisterhood. 

I’d actually like to know what’s an example of an abnormal artist in film? Pollack?
I think this may be the most boring film I have ever seen. I'm down for character studies where not much happens plot-wise, but this was taking the piss. There was nothing to it.

I would say Boyhood (2014) is a portrait of the main character as just an ordinary guy with a passion for photography who creates his portfolio and wants to make a living from it. This is probably cheating, since the end of the film only shows him heading to college with his dreams still intact, and we don’t really know if he will make it as an artist. (I watched this with my son, who had the opposite impression - he figured the main character would end up unemployed).  
Another one would be Impromptu (1991). Hugh Grant plays Frederic Chopin as a mild mannered Polish immigrant with asthma who only wants to play nice music and avoid offending his patrons.

I would disagree but to each their own. My take on the movie is that it’s about a normal person whose life does not resemble a movie and how that’s actually a good thing. William Harper’s character is there as a foil to illustrate the ludicrous nature of people who experience their life as a drama. Patterson instead illuminates the quiet grace and integrity it requires to live a life of routine and simple pleasures.

To the degree that anyone in his films is “normal” given his melodramatic sensibilities, many of Pedro Almodovar’s films more or less fit the bill, including Parallel Mothers, Pain & Glory, Broke Embraces & All About My Mother. Ditto for Mia Hansen-Love, especially Eden and Bergman Island.
[removed]

Have you seen Rivette’s *La belle noiseuse*? It takes place at a painter’s home as the painter uses a model to create a painting that has long been on his mind. You might find it a more “normal” depiction of an artist inasmuch as we see the painter solely in a quiet home life, and though he struggles to paint what he envisioned, his talent isn’t some big horrible curse.

Seconding Bergman Island—beautiful film about how artists can feel caught between their normal lives and what is expected of them both in their art in their relationships. Anatomy of a Fall also explores this, to much darker effect

> the titular character is talented, certainly

I'm not sure I agree, I think Barton is a hack, shown by his play and his script having the same ending.

That’s an interesting reading! It’s been a little while since I’ve seen Barton fink so I’d be interested rewatching it through the lens of him as a hack. Certainly the movie doesn’t go out of its way to portray him as an artist worthy of praise or focus on his art beyond introducing him as acclaimed, however I read him ending his script the same way as a larger gesture towards Hollywood not being a good fit for him, especially considering the toll events in the film take on him.

Still to your point, I think it does a good job of not fetishizing or romanticizing the process. It is largely work, and work he can’t do for most of the film.

Huh? Impossible? That is a feeling I was nowhere near watching that film. A tiny house, a wife with an abundant fascination of their dog (to off putting levels IMO). Certainly the film didn't show passengers yelling at him or the grosser aspects of being a bus driver - which retained some of the dignity of the position but I always assumed all that stuff was in between "the lines" of the film so to speak.

I can't help but feel like any romanticization of low level work like this suggests you have done very little of it yourself. 

I do not say as such to be insulting - hell if you feel a life like that has an impossible amount of dignity your life must be strangely disorienting. Or I'm missing the point completely in which case set me straight.

Chasing Amy, One Crazy Summer, and Ghost World all feature artists as fairly normal.

 As Good as It Gets features a very eccentric writer, but also a very down to Earth painter who just got a bunch of financial problems after a home invasion.

I really enjoyed that movie and was going through a, "I want to learn about underground comics," kick at the time. Watching films based on them, documentaries about them, and reading up a little on them.

What I found interesting is that Robert Crumb hates *American Splendor* the film. In fact, it would appear that Robert Crumb hates every screen adaptation of himself or his work that has ever been made.
Didn't know that about R. Crumb, but I can see it. He doesn't strike me as the type to suffer *anything* gladly.

> however I read him ending his script the same way as a larger gesture towards Hollywood not being a good fit for him

That's an interesting interpretation. 

I think the other more obvious thing that makes me think of Barton as a hack or at least incredibly fake and self-absorbed is the way he constantly ignores the common man (John Goodman) he claims to be writing for and about. If he had listened he might have seen coming everything that follows.

I wonder what your thoughts on Inside Llewyn Davis would be. On one hand I suppose you could view it as a romanticized portrayal of a hapless "tortured artist" archetype, but on the other hand it just feels so grounded and critical of its lead that I think it ultimately avoids those pitfalls and accomplishes that goal of portraying Llewyn as a "normal" flawed person.

My wife and I went on a nice walk after seeing this in the theater. I still think about that walk. I don't think we talked about anything profound, we just talked about how much we both enjoyed watching it. And that we were happy together, and that we liked going out to watch movies. Which I think in a way is what the movie was about.

It's not a dominant part of the movie, but Jack Blacks character in The Holiday is a film composer and he's entirely normal, just a total fanboy. It's beautifully grounded and it's great seeing someone do a very relatable info dump onto someone in the video store scene
[removed]
Frances Ha - it's pretty realistic, in terms of sustainability of being an artist, and how we can still be part of and contribute to the creative community even though we are not 'the star'
[removed]

I detested Showing Up more than I can explain. Maybe it was Michelle Williams playing yet another mopey, whiny, miserable white woman with actually no problems? Again? Is it a commentary on artists or just Michelle Williams doing all she can??

I wouldn't say impossible but I know what they're getting at. I thought the film was a very romantic, hence unrealistic scenario. The simplicity of the plot points and relationships, the contentedness of the couple. The timelessness of the main character and his removal from 21st century signifiers. That's not a criticism, Jarmusch does that kind of very dry fairy tale brilliantly.

I just don't see the romance at all. His, Paterson's, life does not seem enviable on any level. Is the couple content? I am not convinced there aren't things bubbling under the surface.

I guess if romance is what is in question a film like No Lovers Left Alive hits more of the right notes for me (in terms of unrealistic romance).

It's not that I disliked Paterson - I just don't see how it would inspire anyone to become a poet. And maybe true art should discourage one from the act - there's probably a moral that needs to be told in such a way.
I found Frances Ha to be a completely unrealistic, pretentious bore. But that's just me...

I don't know if they fit, but my favourite films about artists:

- Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev. This is the best film about art, creation and being an artist. I can say this with high confidence because it's certainly the best film ever, period. The life of a Russian icon painter in medieval Russia, struggling to find faith in his art amid a violent world. 

- Parajanov's The Color of Pomegranates, about the life of Armenian's poet Sayat Nova

  
Also some movies that I am pretty sure can fit, but are in a lower league than the aforementioned ones:

- Joachim Trier's Reprise and The worst Person in the World are very good movies where you can see normal artist people (writers in the former and cartoonist for the latter)

- Jarmusch's Patterson. A normal guy who also writes poetry
[removed]
Agree lmao

Surprised no one has mentioned Mr. Turner, Mike Leigh’s slice-of-life film about the early 19th century painter J.M.W. Turner, played by Timothy Spall. Topsy-Turvy, Leigh’s film about Gilbert & Sullivan and the making of their musical The Mikado, takes a similar look at working artists and the creative process.
Huh wow never thought about it like this, thanks for sharing

to each his own :) i liked Frances Ha as i felt it resonated with a lot of my and my friends experiences, as most of us are struggling artists.

Opportunities are pretty limited for only the select few, so most of us just find or create pockets of joy where we are. Not everyone is gonna get the 'exhibition slot' or 'star role', so we end up doing adjacent things.

It might not be the same as what we pictured being an 'artist' is like, but that's ok. Some go to the academe, some find work to support other artists, and some do jobs in other fields and do their art on the side. A lot of artists i know go into teaching to make their practices sustainable and still be close to art.

I'm an artist too, and maybe that's why it was so revolting for me. For me, it was too on-the-nose. It wasn't saying anything new either, that previous films before hadn't. It felt like watching a cheap wannabe Woody Allen ripoff. I'm sorry I don't mean to be rude to those who enjoyed it, but like, come on, when that theme from 400 Blows played in one scene, I rolled my eyes so hard. Its a mediocre film, at best.

> no problems

lol
That movie was literally life changing for me, in its portrayal of depression and productivity. Personally validating.

> Personally validating

It totally was/is.

Paterson has a beautiful, supportive, passionate stay-at-home wife who he financially supports on a bus driver's salary.  He writes poetry.  He goes to a pub every night and socializes with his lively community.  He sees like 4 sets of twins in the same week.  He runs into a little girl and an old man who both happen to also love poetry, again in the same week.  He handles every situation with a calm, stoic dignity.  He's not shown having relationship problems, health problems, work problems (his bus breaks down, but this is resolved quickly and doesn't lead to any serious stress), or money problems (money is clearly tight, but this isn't shown causing any stress).  His conversations are mostly mundane, yet don't feel naturalistic like how most people I know talk.

These are the things that feel romanticized by the movie.  It's a strange mix of realism and unrealism.  I get what you mean though, I don't see the perfect happy life that some other people see.  He doesn't seem particularly close (emotionally) with Laura, or anyone else in his life.  He doesn't show much passion.  It's either a totally middle of the road life, or there's a depression bubbling underneath.  Or maybe he's totally content inside while emoting very little externally, idk.

You know that does clarify things for me a little bit. I always put on my fourth wall viewing glasses when I watch movies and take unrealism for granted (since we are already watching something staged). 

Since the movie took me right to the edge of boredom - without toppling in - I assumed boredom was part of the tonal intent. His life isn't great or terrible, it's fine. And the word 'fine' definitely clashes with the word 'impossible', at least in my mind.

Yeah, totally fair.  I think I focus on realism in films to a fault.  I tend to either prefer films that feel totally realistic (particular in the ways the characters act), or films that are explicitly highly stylized, which helps me suspend disbelief.
